idiom_name: TPL Task.Run + await Task.WhenAll (Parallel.Invoke for a fixed group); PLINQ AsParallel for data-parallel leaves
implementation_notes: The Task Parallel Library is the substrate: Task.Run queues a branch on the thread pool, await Task.WhenAll joins the fan-out, and Parallel.Invoke runs a fixed set of statements concurrently - so a recursive decomposition becomes a method that starts its two child calls as tasks and awaits their join. For data-parallel leaves PLINQ replaces the recursion entirely: AsParallel() partitions the source into segments and runs the query on worker threads, with Parallel.ForEach/For as the imperative equivalent. Await the join (never Task.Wait or .Result) and keep the sequential cut-off, since every level of Task.Run doubles the queued tasks while the leaf work shrinks.
pitfalls: Blocking on a task (Task.Wait, .Result) inside code with a synchronisation context can deadlock; await Task.WhenAll instead.
Unbounded Task.Run per recursion level floods the thread pool queue with tiny tasks; keep the cut-off and consider Parallel.ForEach over chunks.
PLINQ is not free: partitioning and merging cost, .AsOrdered forces synchronisation, and non-thread-safe delegates (shared Random, mutable accumulators) produce wrong results.
